manifest.name: dsh-screenshot
manifest.description: Quick Shot / Screenshot question for DeepSeek Harness: one-click capture from the composer, an adjustable selection frame with eight handles, and the crop lands directly as an image attachment. Captures exclude the Harness window itself.

readme.text:
A **screenshot-and-ask** plugin for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH).

One click in the composer captures the screen, a frozen frame appears with a
box you can drag and then fine-tune, and the crop lands in your message as an
ordinary image attachment — ready for the question you were about to type.

Unlike most capture tools, the frame **excludes the Harness window itself**, so
you can point at whatever is behind it.

Asking a question about something on screen usually means: take a screenshot
with the system tool, find the file, drag it into the chat, then type. Four
steps and a detour through the filesystem. This collapses that to one click.

The overlay is an in-page surface, not an OS window, so nothing is left behind:
no tray entry, no floating window, no files to clean up.

- **One click, no dialog** — the camera button sits in the composer's tool row.
- **Adjustable selection** — after the first drag the frame stays, with eight
  handles (four corners, four edges) and a draggable interior. Move it until it
  is right; nothing is cropped until you confirm.
- **Confirm by button or key** — `Enter` or the confirm button; `Esc`,
  right-click, or the cancel button discard the whole capture.
- **Live size readout** in real pixels, not screen pixels.
- **Harness window excluded** — the app's own windows are minimized for the
  freeze and restored immediately after, so the frame holds only other
  applications.
- **Fast** — a resident capture helper keeps a warm process, the window list is
  cached, and the freeze settles in ~45 ms instead of 320 ms, so a whole capture
  is roughly 130–180 ms. See [Performance](#performance).
- **Smooth** — the selection is one element with a `box-shadow` dim, and pointer
  moves are coalesced to one commit per animation frame, so the frame tracks the
  cursor at display rate instead of refreshing the DOM on every event.
- **Nothing to clean up** — the crop goes straight into the draft as a browser
  attachment; no screensh

- **Windows** — the capture helper uses PowerShell 5.1 with WinForms and GDI+.
- **DSH** with the Web GUI (`dsh web` or the desktop app). The plugin needs the
  `webServer` Host service and the Conversation Client services, both present in
  a standard web profile.
- A model that accepts images, if you want the model to see the crop.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:<your-account>/dsh-screenshot
```

Then restart DSH so the Host half registers its route and starts the helper.

For local development, install the directory instead:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add ./dsh-screenshot
```

1. Click the camera button at the left of the composer tool row.
2. The screen freezes. Drag to sketch the area you want to ask about.
3. Release. The frame stays — drag its edges, corners, or interior to adjust.
4. Press `Enter` or click **Confirm**. `Esc`, right-click, or **Cancel** discards.
5. The crop appears as an image attachment in your draft. Type your question and send.

Two halves, one flow.

**Host half** (`index.js`) owns a long-lived PowerShell helper
(`scripts/capture.ps1`) and two exact-match same-origin HTTP routes,
`/api/dsh-screenshot/capture` and `/api/dsh-screenshot/crop`. The helper reads
newline frames on stdin:

| Frame in | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<id>\|ping` | health check |
| `<id>\|shot\|<hideApp>\|<hideDelayMs>` | capture one frame |
| `<id>\|crop\|<srcPath>\|<l>,<t>,<w>,<h>\|<dstPath>` | cut one rectangle out of a frame |

and answers `OK\|<id>\|<w>\|<h>\|<bytes>\|<path>\|<sx>\|<sy>\|<sw>\|<sh>`
or `ERR\|<id>\|<reason>`.

Before freezing, the helper minimizes every visible top-level window owned by
this app, waits for the frame to settle, captures the virtual desktop, then restores
each window to its previous state and foreground. The routes require the
application's own auth cookie, so an unrelated page on the machine cannot read
the screen through them. Capture answers with the raw PNG bytes plus
`x-shot-width`, `x-shot-height` and `x-shot-id` headers; crop answers with the
raw PNG bytes of the rectangle plus `x-crop-width` and `x-crop-height`.

Frames stay on disk between the two calls (at most six, oldest evicted) so the
crop never has to round-trip the pixels through the browser. Each frame is
consumed by one crop and deleted with it.

**Client half** (`client.js`) registers two slots:

- `conversation.input.left` — the camera button.
- `shell.overlay` — the frozen-frame selection surface, mounted only while a
  capture is pending.

On confirm, the selection is mapped back to the screenshot's own pixels through
the same `object-fit: contain` letterbox math used to display it, and the Host
cuts that rectangle out of the frame it already holds. The result is handed to
the composer as a `File` through the Conversation service's draft attachments.
It behaves exactly like a pasted picture.

A capture was profiled step by step, because "it feels slow" turned out to be
four separate costs rather than one. Measured on a 2560×1600 desktop at 150% DPI:

| Step | First cut | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `Get-Process` window-owner sweep | 79 ms | 0 (cached, 20 s TTL) |
| `EnumWindows` | 25 ms | 0 (cached, verified with `IsWindow`) |
| Wait for the minimize animation | 320 ms | **45 ms** |
| `CopyFromScreen` 2560×1600 | 45 ms | 45 ms |
| PNG encode | 45 ms | 45 ms (buffer reused) |
| Post-restore settle sleep | 80 ms | 0 (restore is async) |
| **Total** | **≈520–600 ms** | **≈130–180 ms** |

The other half was the Client:

- The route used to answer with the PNG **base64'd inside JSON**, so the browser had to parse a multi-megabyte string and then base64-decode a `data:` URL before the first pixel could appear. It now answers `image/png` and the Client hands `URL.createObjectURL` straight to ``, revoking it on teardown. - The overlay used to be mounted only *after* `requestFullscreen()` resolved, which put Chromium's full-screen animation in front of the user. The freeze is now shown first and the window widens behind it (`measure()` re-runs on `fullscreenchange`). - The dim was four separately positioned translucent rectangles repainted on every pointer move. It is now a single `box-shadow: 0 0 0 100vmax` spread on the selection frame itself, with the eight handles as CSS-positioned children, so one element's geometry change is the entire per-frame cost. - `getBoundingClientRect()` was called on every pointer move (a forced layout). The overlay is `position: fixed; inset: 0`, so viewport coordinates already are layer coordinates.

And one cost that only showed up *after* confirming, as a delay before the
picture appeared in the composer:

- The crop used to run in the browser — `drawImage` of a four-megapixel frame
  into a canvas, then `canvas.toBlob('image/png')` — both on the renderer's main
  thread, in the same breath as the composer repaint and the window leaving full
  screen. The pixels were already on disk, so the crop moved there: the warm
  helper cuts the rectangle out with GDI+ and streams the PNG back. Attaching was
  never the slow part; the composer only builds an object URL and defers the
  bytes to send time.

No configuration. The plugin registers no `Config` schema and reads no files
outside the workspace.

```
dsh-screenshot/
├── index.js             # Host half: helper lifecycle + capture route
├── client.js            # Client half: camera button + selection overlay
├── scripts/capture.ps1  # Resident PowerShell helper (WinForms + GDI+)

- **Windows only.** The Host half has no capture backend for macOS or Linux, so
  the route answers with an error there.
- **One screen, whole desktop.** Multi-monitor setups are captured as one
  virtual desktop image; the selection frame spans all of them.
- **Independent PowerShell consoles** may still appear in the frame even when
  hidden, depending on how their host renders them.
- Hiding the app's windows momentarily changes focus; the previous foreground
  window is restored right after the capture.

- The capture route requires the app's auth cookie and is exact-match only.
- The screenshot is processed in memory and handed to the composer as an
  attachment; the helper's temporary PNG is deleted as soon as it is read.
- No network calls, no bundled keys, no external services.
